title: Bell Labs 1947: point-contact and junction transistors
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE TRANSISTOR
SECTION 5.2. BELL LABS 1947: POINT-CONTACT AND JUNCTION TRANSISTORS

On December 23, 1947, in a laboratory at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain demonstrated to colleagues a small device made of a germanium crystal, a plastic wedge and a strip of gold foil that amplified an audio signal. It was the first transistor. Within a few weeks their group leader, William Shockley, conceived a better design, the junction transistor, which became the workhorse of electronics in the 1950s and 1960s. This section tells the story and explains how a bipolar junction transistor amplifies and switches, using the p-n junction physics of Section 5.1.

1. The motivation: replacing tubes and relays

The American telephone system, run by AT&T with Bell Labs as its research arm, depended on millions of vacuum tubes (in long-distance amplifiers) and relays (in switching exchanges). Tubes consumed power, burned out, and needed warm-up time; relays were slow and wore out. Mervin Kelly, Bell Labs' director of research, wanted a solid-state replacement, and after the war he organized a solid-state physics group with Shockley as one of its leaders. The group included the experimental physicist Walter Brattain (1902-1987), a long-time Bell Labs researcher in surface physics, and the theorist John Bardeen (1908-1991), who joined in 1945.

2. The first idea: a field-effect device, and why it failed

The obvious idea, which Shockley pursued in 1945, was a field-effect amplifier: put a metal plate near the surface of a thin semiconductor layer and apply a voltage to the plate. The electric field should attract or repel carriers in the semiconductor, changing its conductivity, just as a tube's grid controls current. This principle had actually been patented by Julius Edgar Lilienfeld, who filed in Canada in 1925, and by Oskar Heil in 1934, but neither produced a practical device that industry adopted.

When Shockley's group tried it, the effect was far smaller than theory predicted. Bardeen explained why in 1946-1947: electrons were trapped in "surface states" at the semiconductor surface, and these trapped charges screened the interior from the applied field. Understanding and controlling surfaces became the group's central research problem. (The field-effect transistor would succeed only around 1959-1960, when the silicon-silicon dioxide interface solved the surface-state problem. That device, the MOSFET, is Section 5.3's main subject and the basis of all modern chips.)

3. The point-contact transistor (December 1947)

Experimenting with surface states, Brattain and Bardeen found in November and December 1947 that the way charges near a point contact on germanium behaved could be exploited directly. In mid-December Brattain wrapped a strip of gold foil around the edge of a triangular plastic wedge, slit the foil at the tip with a razor to make two contacts very close together (separated by a tiny fraction of a millimeter), and pressed the wedge onto a germanium crystal sitting on a metal base.

  - One gold contact was biased slightly positive relative to the base: the emitter.
  - The other was biased negative: the collector.
  - The germanium block and its metal base formed the third terminal: the base.

A small change in emitter current produced a larger change in collector current, and with an appropriate load resistor this gave voltage and power gain. Brattain's notebook records voltage gain on December 15; by December 16 they had power amplification, and on the afternoon of December 23, 1947, they demonstrated the device to Bell Labs managers by amplifying speech. That date is usually given as the birth of the transistor.

What was happening, in modern terms: the emitter contact injected holes (minority carriers in the n-type germanium) into the region near the surface, and these holes flowed to the collector, increasing its current. The device worked by minority carrier injection, a mechanism nobody had clearly anticipated.

The name. Bell Labs needed a name. Proposals included "semiconductor triode" and "iotatron." "Transistor," suggested by the engineer John R. Pierce, won an internal vote; it combines "transfer" and "resistor" (in the sense of transresistance).

Announcement. Bell Labs kept the work confidential while it filed patents and announced the transistor publicly on June 30, 1948. Press reaction was modest; few understood its significance.

Independent invention in France. In Europe, the German physicists Herbert Matare and Heinrich Welker, working for a Westinghouse subsidiary near Paris, independently developed a point-contact amplifier based on the same minority-carrier injection effect and filed a patent on August 13, 1948. They called it the "transistron," and it was manufactured for French telephone and military use. Matare had observed related effects earlier while working on radar diodes in wartime Germany.

The point-contact transistor was difficult to make reproducibly, noisy, and fragile, since its performance depended on the exact pressure and position of the contacts. Western Electric (AT&T's manufacturing arm) nonetheless began producing it on a production line in Allentown, Pennsylvania, on October 1, 1951. It found uses in telephone equipment and hearing aids and in some early transistor computers.

4. Shockley's junction transistor (1948)

Shockley, reportedly frustrated that the breakthrough had been made by his subordinates without him, worked intensely on a theory of how such devices worked and in January 1948 conceived a fundamentally different and better structure: a sandwich of three regions of doped semiconductor, n-p-n or p-n-p, with two p-n junctions back to back. This is the bipolar junction transistor (BJT). His theory was published in 1949, and the book "Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors" (1950) became a foundational text.

Making junction transistors required controlling doping precisely within a single crystal. Gordon Teal and Morgan Sparks at Bell Labs did this by changing the dopant in the melt while growing a crystal, producing "grown-junction" transistors around 1950-1951. Other methods followed: alloy junctions, then diffused junctions, which allowed very thin base regions and much higher speeds.

In 1956 Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the Nobel Prize in Physics "for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect." (Bardeen won a second physics Nobel in 1972 for the theory of superconductivity.)

5. How a bipolar junction transistor works

Take an n-p-n transistor: an n-type emitter (heavily doped), a thin p-type base (lightly doped), and an n-type collector.

    Emitter (n+) | Base (p, thin) | Collector (n)
         E               B               C

In normal amplifying operation ("forward active mode"):

  - The base-emitter junction is forward biased (Vbe about 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon).
  - The base-collector junction is reverse biased (collector more positive than base).

Step by step:

  1. Forward bias on the B-E junction lowers its barrier. The heavily doped emitter injects a large number of electrons into the base. (Holes also flow from base into emitter, but because the emitter is much more heavily doped, this is a small fraction.)
  2. In the base, these electrons are minority carriers. The base is very thin, much thinner than the distance electrons travel before recombining with holes, so most electrons diffuse across it without recombining.
  3. When they reach the reverse-biased B-C junction, the strong electric field in its depletion region sweeps them into the collector.

So most of the current injected by the emitter arrives at the collector. Only a small base current is needed, to supply the holes that recombine in the base and those injected into the emitter.

The key equations (simplified, ignoring the Early effect):

    Ic = Is * exp( Vbe / VT )                (exponential, like a diode)
    Ib = Ic / beta
    Ie = Ic + Ib

where beta (also written hFE) is the current gain, typically 50 to several hundred. The exponential dependence on Vbe comes straight from the p-n junction physics of Section 5.1.

Transconductance. Differentiating:

    gm = dIc / dVbe = Ic / VT

At Ic = 1 mA, gm = 1 mA / 25.9 mV, about 39 mA/V, much larger than a typical vacuum tube's few mA/V. That is one reason transistors make efficient amplifiers.

6. The BJT as a switch

For digital logic we use the transistor in two extreme regions, as with tubes:

  Cutoff: Vbe below about 0.5 V. Essentially no collector current; the switch is off.

  Saturation: base current large enough that the collector voltage falls to about 0.1 to 0.2 V above the emitter (both junctions forward biased). The transistor acts like a closed switch with a small voltage drop.

The common-emitter inverter: emitter to ground, collector to supply Vcc through a resistor Rc, input through a resistor Rb to the base.

  - Input low (0 V): transistor cut off, Ic = 0, output = Vcc. High.
  - Input high (say 5 V): base current Ib = (5 - 0.7) / Rb. If beta * Ib > Vcc / Rc, the transistor saturates, output about 0.2 V. Low.

Design example: Vcc = 5 V, Rc = 1 kOhm, so the saturated collector current is about (5 - 0.2) / 1000, 4.8 mA. With beta at least 50, we need Ib at least 4.8 mA / 50, 0.096 mA. Choose Rb = 10 kOhm: Ib = 4.3 / 10,000 = 0.43 mA, giving a safety factor of about 4.5 to tolerate low-beta parts. This is exactly how you would drive a relay coil or LED from a microcontroller pin with an NPN transistor, though for a relay you must add a flyback diode across the coil.

Speed limit. Saturation has a cost: excess minority carriers stored in the base must be removed before the transistor can turn off, which delays switching (storage time). Logic families such as ECL (emitter-coupled logic) avoided saturation entirely to switch faster, and Schottky-clamped TTL used a Schottky diode to keep transistors just out of deep saturation (Section 5.3).

7. Transistors versus tubes

    Property             Vacuum tube (triode)            Transistor (BJT, 1950s)
    --------             --------------------            -----------------------
    Heater power         about 1 W or more, always on    none
    Supply voltage       tens to hundreds of volts       a few volts to tens
    Size                 centimeters                     millimeters (soon microns)
    Warm-up              seconds                         instant
    Lifetime             thousands of hours              essentially unlimited if not overstressed
    Shock resistance     fragile glass                   rugged
    Early weaknesses     -                               temperature sensitivity, variability, cost

Early germanium transistors had problems: they leaked significantly at high temperatures, characteristics varied from device to device, and they were expensive at first. Silicon handled heat far better because of its wider band gap, and the first silicon transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs by Morris Tanenbaum on January 26, 1954, with Gordon Teal (by then at Texas Instruments) independently producing silicon transistors a few months later. Germanium remained dominant until the late 1950s, when silicon took over.

8. First products

  - Hearing aids were among the earliest consumer uses, from the early 1950s, because battery life mattered so much.
  - The Regency TR-1 (1954), using Texas Instruments transistors, is generally regarded as the first commercially produced transistor radio. Sony's transistor radios later in the 1950s made the company's name.
  - Military electronics, especially for missiles and aircraft, were major early customers because of weight, power and ruggedness.
  - Computers adopted transistors from the mid-1950s (Section 5.4).

9. Aftermath: Shockley and Silicon Valley

Shockley left Bell Labs in 1955-1956 and founded Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory in Mountain View, California, near Stanford, hiring talented young scientists and engineers. His management style was difficult, and in 1957 eight of them, including Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, left to found Fairchild Semiconductor. Fairchild developed the planar process and one of the first practical integrated circuits (Section 6.1), and its alumni later founded Intel and many other companies. The concentration of semiconductor firms in the area gave it the name Silicon Valley. (Shockley's later years were marred by his promotion of racist views on intelligence and genetics, which were widely condemned.)

10. Summary

  - Bell Labs sought a solid-state replacement for tubes and relays; an early field-effect approach failed because of surface states, explained by Bardeen.
  - Bardeen and Brattain's germanium point-contact transistor showed power gain in mid-December 1947 and was demonstrated on December 23, 1947; it was announced on June 30, 1948, and named by John R. Pierce.
  - Matare and Welker independently developed the "transistron" in France (patent filed August 13, 1948).
  - Shockley conceived the bipolar junction transistor in January 1948; grown junctions came around 1950-1951; the first silicon transistor was made at Bell Labs on January 26, 1954.
  - A BJT works by minority carrier injection across a thin base: Ic = Is exp(Vbe / VT), Ib = Ic / beta, gm = Ic / VT.
  - As a switch it operates between cutoff and saturation; the three inventors shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
